issues.legal_issue: A quarry lease described only as being for limestone for burning is not void if the lease documents and surrounding circumstances show that it concerns limestone classified as a minor mineral.
material_facts: The lease described the mineral as “limestone for burning,” wording that could cover either a minor or a major mineral.
The lease was granted under the rules for minor minerals, pursuant to an order treating it as a minor-mineral lease, and used the prescribed lease form.
The royalty and other terms of the lease were consistent with a lease for a minor mineral, namely limestone used in kilns to manufacture lime for use as building material.
issues.conclusion: The lease was for a minor mineral and could not be declared void merely because it described the mineral as “limestone for burning.”
issues.legal_principle: Under section 3(e) of the Mines and Minerals (Regulation and Development) Act, 1957, the Central Government may declare a mineral to be a minor mineral. The 1958 notification covered limestone used for lime burning generally; the 1961 amendment narrowed the category to limestone used in kilns to manufacture lime for use as building material. Because the description “limestone for burning” is ambiguous, the mineral’s classification must be assessed from the lease’s other provisions and the circumstances of its execution. The Madhya Pradesh Minor Minerals Rules, 1961, including rule 29, the prescribed lease form, the royalty schedule, and the Third Schedule, supported the conclusion that this lease concerned a minor mineral. No earlier cases were relied on.

predicates.quarry_lease_validity_disputed: A party challenges whether a quarry lease is valid because the mineral is said to fall outside the category governed by the applicable lease rules.
predicates.ambiguous_mineral_description: The lease describes the mineral in terms that could refer to more than one legal category of mineral.
predicates.lease_context_indicates_minor_mineral: The lease’s terms, the process by which it was granted, or related documents indicate that it concerns a mineral governed by the rules for minor-mineral leases.

issues.definition: When a challenged lease uses an ambiguous mineral description but its surrounding context indicates a minor-mineral lease, the lease is not void on the basis of that description alone.

issues.legal_issue: An application adequately identifies the mineral sought when its description is sufficiently specific to show that the application concerns a minor mineral.
material_facts: The application described the mineral as “limestone for burning as a minor mineral.”

That description distinguished the mineral sought from limestone for burning that would be classified as a major mineral and identified the intended category as limestone used in kilns to make lime for building material.
issues.conclusion: The application was sufficiently specific and was a proper application in respect of a minor mineral; it was wrongly rejected on the ground that it sought a major mineral.
issues.legal_principle: The requirement in Form I, paragraph 3, column 6 of the Madhya Pradesh Minor Minerals Rules, 1961, that an applicant state the mineral intended to be mined serves to identify the mineral sought. If the description is sufficient for that purpose, the application is not vague or indefinite merely because it does not repeat the mineral’s full formal description. The description must still identify a mineral within section 3(e) of the Mines and Minerals (Regulation and Development) Act, 1957, as applied by the relevant Central Government notification. No earlier cases were relied on.

predicates.minor_mineral_lease_application: An applicant seeks a lease governed by rules for minor-mineral leases.
predicates.mineral_description_identifies_requested: The application describes the mineral sufficiently to identify what the applicant seeks to mine, including its relevant category.

issues.definition: If an application for a minor-mineral lease identifies the mineral sought, its description is sufficiently specific.

issues.legal_issue: A lessee cannot obtain renewal of a quarry lease when the lease contains no option of renewal.
material_facts: The lessee applied to renew a quarry lease that did not contain an option of renewal.
The lease form’s renewal-option clause had been deleted.
issues.conclusion: The renewal application was misconceived and could be rejected, notwithstanding that its description of the mineral was adequate.
issues.legal_principle: A lessee may seek renewal on the basis of an option only where the lease grants such an option. In the absence of an option, the applicant may seek a fresh lease but cannot claim renewal. The Court applied the terms of the lease in the context of the prescribed lease form under the Madhya Pradesh Minor Minerals Rules, 1961. No earlier cases were relied on.

predicates.quarry_lease_renewal_application: A lessee applies to renew an existing quarry lease.
predicates.lease_contains_renewal_option: The lease gives the lessee an option to obtain a renewal.

issues.definition: When a lessee applies to renew a quarry lease that gives no renewal option, the renewal application may be rejected.

issues.legal_issue: An appellate court will not entertain a challenge to a lease grant that was not raised before the relevant administrative authority or the High Court.
material_facts: A later application for a fresh lease was pending when the authority granted a lease to another applicant.

The appellant argued that the grant was invalid because the authority had not considered the pending application, and the rules permitted a later application to be preferred for special recorded reasons.
The appellant had not raised this contention before the administrative authority or the High Court, although opportunities to do so were available.
issues.conclusion: The Court did not entertain the contention or interfere with the lease grant on that ground, despite observing that the authority appeared to have erred by ignoring the pending application.
issues.legal_principle: Rule 12(2) of the Madhya Pradesh Minor Minerals Rules, 1961 permitted the authority, for special reasons to be recorded, to grant a quarry lease to a later applicant in preference to an earlier applicant. The Court considered that the pending application ought to have been considered, but declined to interfere because the appellant had not raised the contention before the authority or the High Court. No earlier cases were relied on.

predicates.appeal_from_lease_grant: A party appeals from a decision granting a lease to another applicant.
predicates.contention_not_raised_before_administrat: The party did not present the contention to the administrative authority before appealing.
predicates.contention_not_raised_before_high_court: The party did not present the contention to the High Court before pursuing a further appeal.

issues.definition: In an appeal from a lease grant, a contention omitted before both the administrative authority and the High Court is not entertained for the first time in the further appeal.

issues.legal_issue: A government secretary may extend the time for executing a lease as an exercise of the government’s authority under its rules of business, even without a delegation of that power to the secretary.
material_facts: The rules allowed the State Government to permit execution of a lease after the prescribed period if the applicant was not responsible for the delay.
The appellant contended that the secretary lacked authority because the State Government had not delegated the extension power to that officer.
The secretary extended the time as an exercise of the State Government’s authority under the Rules of Business, not as a delegate.
issues.conclusion: The extension order was an order of the State Government and was not invalid for lack of delegated authority.
issues.legal_principle: The proviso to rule 22 of the Madhya Pradesh Minor Minerals Rules, 1961 empowered the State Government to permit execution of a lease after the prescribed period in the specified circumstances. An officer acting under the State Government’s Rules of Business exercises the State Government’s authority in making such an order; the order does not depend on a delegation of power to that officer. No earlier cases were relied on.

predicates.challenge_to_lease_execution_extension: A party challenges an order extending the time allowed to execute a lease.
predicates.no_delegation_to_secretary: The government had not separately delegated the extension power to the secretary who made the order.
predicates.secretary_acted_under_rules_of_business: The secretary made the order by exercising the government’s authority under its rules of business rather than acting as a delegate.

issues.definition: An extension order made by a secretary under the government’s rules of business remains a government order even when the secretary has not received a separate delegation.
